RELEVANT CHARACTER BACKGROUND

Aminata Diallo is a young working-class woman living in a rented room in a busy district on the outskirts of Bamako, in a home with packed-earth walls, a corrugated tin roof, and no tap water. She rises before dawn, fills a bucket at a communal stand two blocks away, and carries it back carefully so she does not spill water on her only pair of work trousers. She works six days a week on a construction crew and is the youngest person there and the only woman. Her master mason, Sékou, has taught her the trade over two years and trusts her with load calculations; he teases her as la petite comptable because she mentally recalculates estimates before lifting a trowel. He has also lent her a textbook after learning she studies accounting. His wife has never met Aminata directly but sends greetings through him.

Aminata is also an accounting student preparing for an exam at a community center on the other side of the city. She studies at night by kerosene lamp after long workdays and often walks rather than pay bus fare. She keeps a small notebook tucked inside her shirt with figures and dates and maintains an emergency fund hidden under a loose floorboard near her mattress, adding the same amount each month and never touching it. She is saving carefully for a proper room with running water so her younger sister can live with her and attend school. Her money is limited, and she cannot afford bus fare across town for every trip. She accepts only invitations that do not require extra bus fare.

Her values are centered on careful accounting, self-reliance, financial caution, and verification. She learned to double-check everything after watching her mother lose a market stall to a miscalculated loan. Her mother died when Aminata was twelve. She also once watched her father sell his tools to pay for a funeral and never hold a trowel again. These experiences shaped a strong habit of checking, counting, and relying on what she has verified herself. She counts bricks, rice costs, weeks until exams, and even her steps while walking. She treats counted and checked quantities as the only trustworthy basis for decisions.

Her response style is quiet, restrained, precise, and highly self-monitoring. She does not laugh off teasing, usually responds with a nod, and does not speak openly about private plans. She is disciplined and persistent, continuing to work and study despite fatigue. She has declined three previous social invitations this month in order to study, citing fatigue. She walks past food stalls without buying in order to save money for her sister’s room.

OBJECTIVE SITUATION

After a long day at the construction site, Aminata is packing her trowel when Sékou approaches her and says that his wife has prepared a large pot of yassa poulet for the neighborhood’s Korité celebration. He invites her to join his family for the meal that night. Aminata is exhausted and had planned to study for her accounting exam by lamplight. She knows that declining a meal invitation during Korité can seem rude, but she also does not want to spend money on bus fare across town or lose time away from her books. She must decide whether to accept or politely decline.

Aminata is physically depleted from work: her shoulders ache from hauling cement, her right hand is blistered where the trowel handle rubbed, and she has not eaten since a piece of bread at dawn. Her exam notes are tucked inside her shirt and are damp with sweat. She is carrying the immediate demands of fatigue, hunger, and study materials while standing at the site at the end of the day.

The smell of yassa poulet directly cues a memory of the last Korité before her mother died, when they ate together at a neighbor’s table. Sékou’s phrase “my wife has prepared” echoes the way her mother used to announce a meal.
